Let \(T=(x,y,z)\) be any triple of nonnegative reals satisfying a nontrivial integer relation. We establish the following lemma by descent.

Choose a relation \(a x+b y+c z=0\) with minimal positive \(L=|a|+|b|+|c|\). If a coordinate is zero, stop. Otherwise signs are mixed; after relabeling and moving terms, write
\[
p x+q y=r z\quad(p,q,r>0).
\]
Order the numbers so that x\le y\le z. Equal numbers give 0 in one move. For distinct numbers, subtract the smaller of x,y from z. Substitution \(z=z'+x\) or \(z=z'+y\) changes the corresponding coefficient by adding or subtracting r. Choose the subtraction for which the coefficient has opposite sign to r. The elementary identity
\[
|m-r|+r\le |m|+r,
\]
with strict inequality when 0<m<2r, shows that after at most two such legal subtractions the resulting integer relation has strictly smaller \(\ell^1\)-norm. (If the first subtraction makes the selected coefficient zero, the descent is immediate.)

Thus, unless zero has already appeared, we obtain another triple satisfying a nontrivial integer relation with a smaller positive integer norm. Repeating is impossible indefinitely. At the final norm 1, the relation is \(\pm x_i=0\), so a zero must have appeared.

Taking \(T=(r_1,r_2,r_3)\) proves the assertion.
